```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Counts are often grouped: crash counts by road segment and year, segments
within counties, animal counts by site and survey. Observations in the same
group share unmeasured conditions, so they are correlated, and the groups
themselves are of interest. `countreg_hier()` fits **hierarchical**
(mixed-effects, multilevel) count models with normally distributed random
effects at any number of grouping levels, nested or crossed, for any count
family of the package.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("stream_salamanders")
s <- stream_salamanders
s$sample <- factor(s$sample)
```

The salamander data have 644 counts from 23 stream sites, each surveyed
four times (`sample`), for seven species and life stages (`spp`), at sites
affected or not by mountaintop mining (`mined`).

## 1. A random intercept

Random-effect terms are written as in lme4: `(1 | site)` gives each site
its own intercept, $b_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$:

```{r fit}
h <- countreg_hier(count ~ spp + mined + (1 | site), data = s,
                   family = "NB2")
summary(h)
```

The model is

$$
\log \mu_{ij} = x_{ij}'\beta + b_j, \qquad
y_{ij} \mid b_j \sim \text{NB2}(\mu_{ij}, \alpha), \qquad
b_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
$$

and the likelihood integrates each site's $b_j$ out. With one grouping
factor the integral is computed by **adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature**
(9 points by default), which is accurate even for small groups.

The standard deviation 0.54 means that sites with the same covariates
differ in their expected counts by a factor of about
$\exp(2 \times 0.54) \approx 3$ between the 16th and 84th percentiles.
`re_lrtest()` tests whether the variance is zero. The null value is on the
boundary of the parameter space, so the p-value is half that of the usual
$\chi^2_1$ test:

```{r lrtest}
re_lrtest(h)
```

## 2. Effects of the groups

`ranef()` returns the conditional modes of the site effects, the most
likely value of each site's effect given its counts. They are shrunk
towards zero, more so for sites with little information. `VarCorr()`
returns the estimated variance components and `fixef()` the fixed
coefficients:

```{r ranef}
head(ranef(h)$site)
VarCorr(h)
```

## 3. Crossed and nested effects

Several terms can be combined. Here the site effects are **crossed** with
survey occasions shared by all sites:

```{r crossed}
h2 <- countreg_hier(count ~ spp + mined + (1 | site) + (1 | sample),
                    data = s, family = "POISSON")
VarCorr(h2)
```

**Nested** effects, such as surveys within sites, are written
`(1 | site/sample)`, which is short for `(1 | site) + (1 | site:sample)`.
With more than one term the model uses the **Laplace approximation** with
sparse matrices, as `lme4::glmer()` and `glmmTMB` do. It handles thousands
of groups at several levels.

## 4. Random slopes

`(1 + cover | site)` gives each site its own intercept and its own effect
of `cover`, with a correlation between them. `(cover || site)` makes them
uncorrelated:

```{r slopes}
h3 <- countreg_hier(count ~ cover + mined + (cover || site), data = s,
                    family = "NB2")
VarCorr(h3)
```

The slope's standard deviation is estimated at zero, so `cover` has the
same effect at every site. A variance on the boundary is a **singular
fit**: `summary()` says so, and the Wald standard errors of that term's
variance components are not reported, since they are not meaningful
there. Remove the term, or test it with `re_lrtest()`.

Group-level predictors (such as `mined`, constant within sites) are
ordinary columns of the formula, and cross-level interactions such as
`mined:cover` are ordinary interactions.

## 5. Predictions

`predict()` conditions on the estimated effects of the groups by default.
`re.form` chooses which levels to condition on (`NA` for none), and groups
not seen in estimation get no effect:

```{r predict}
nd <- s[c(1, 30), ]
predict(h2, newdata = nd)                         # site and sample
predict(h2, newdata = nd, re.form = ~ (1 | site)) # site only
predict(h2, newdata = nd, re.form = NA)           # population level
```

A population-level prediction with the effects at zero is the expected
count of a *median* site. The **mean** over sites is larger: for the log
link it is $\exp(\eta + \sigma^2/2)$. `marginal = TRUE` integrates the
effects that are not conditioned on out of the mean:

```{r marginal}
predict(h2, newdata = nd, re.form = NA, marginal = TRUE)
```

`simulate()` draws new counts, either for the same groups
(`use_re = "conditional"`) or for new groups with new effects
(`use_re = "new"`).

## 6. Predictions from a separate history

To forecast a new period, the effects of the groups should come from
their past counts, not from the counts being forecast. `history` gives
the past data: the effects of its groups are computed from those counts
alone, at the fitted parameters, and groups without history are treated
as new groups.

```{r history}
data("washington_roads")
w <- washington_roads
past <- w[w$Year < 2018, ]
h_w <- countreg_hier(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength) +
                       (1 | ID), data = past, family = "POISSON")
next_year <- w[w$Year == 2018, ]
last_year <- past[past$Year == 2017, ]
head(cbind(
  all_years = predict(h_w, newdata = next_year),
  last_year = predict(h_w, newdata = next_year, history = last_year),
  observed  = next_year$Total_crashes))
```

## 7. Intervals for the variance components

Wald intervals for a standard deviation are symmetric and can cross zero.
Profile-likelihood intervals follow the likelihood, so they are asymmetric
and stop at zero:

```{r profile}
confint(h, "sd_(Intercept)|site")                      # Wald
confint(h, "sd_(Intercept)|site", method = "profile")  # profile
```

Each profile point refits the model, so a profile interval takes several
fits per limit.

## 8. Smooth terms

The fixed part can contain penalized smooths, `s()` and `t2()`. They are
fitted in their mixed-model form (as in gamm4): the wiggly part of each
smooth is a set of normal random coefficients whose variance is
$1/\lambda$, so the smoothness is estimated by the marginal likelihood
together with the other variance components.

```{r smooth}
hs <- countreg_hier(count ~ mined + s(cover) + (1 | site), data = s,
                    family = "POISSON")
hs$model$smooth_table[, c("term", "edf", "p.value")]
```

`plot_smooths()`, `smooth_estimates()` and the other smooth tools of
`vignette("smooth-effects")` work as for `countreg()`. Here the effect of
`cover` is linear (EDF 1).

## 9. Non-normal random effects

With one grouping term, the effects can have other distributions, through
`re_dist`, and the likelihood is computed by simulation
(`engine = "msl"`, `re_draws` draws per group):

* `"uniform"` and `"triangular"`: effects with mean zero and the reported
  standard deviation, with bounded support;
* `"gamma"`: the group's multiplicative effect $\exp(b_j)$ is gamma with
  mean 1, as in the classic negative binomial random-effects model. With
  a Poisson family this is `repois()`, computed by simulation.

```{r gamma}
hg <- countreg_hier(count ~ spp + mined + (1 | site), data = s,
                    family = "POISSON", re_dist = "gamma")
rp <- repois(count ~ spp + mined, group_var = "site", data = s,
             method = "BFGS")
c(simulated = logLik(hg), closed_form = logLik(rp))
```

Group effects from the simulation engine are posterior means. The gamma
distribution needs a gamma quantile for every draw, so it is slower than
the others.

## 10. Correlated random effects

Random effects are assumed independent of the covariates. `cre` adds the
group means of time-varying covariates (Mundlak's device), which absorbs
that correlation, and `cre_test()` tests it:

```{r cre}
hc <- countreg_hier(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength) +
                      (1 | ID), data = w, family = "POISSON", cre = ~ lnaadt)
cre_test(hc)
```

## 11. Families and engines

Every count family can be used, including user-defined families
(`new_count_family()`), and the distribution parameters can depend on
covariates (`dis_param_formula_1`, `dis_param_formula_2`). For the
Poisson, NB1 and NB2 families the derivatives of the log-density are
analytic; for the others they are computed numerically.

`engine` chooses the integration method:

| engine | when | method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"aghq"` | one grouping term | adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature, `nAGQ` points per effect |
| `"laplace"` | any terms, nested or crossed; smooth terms | Laplace approximation |
| `"msl"` | one grouping term, any `re_dist` | maximum simulated likelihood |
| `"auto"` (default) | | `"msl"` for non-normal effects, `"aghq"` for one term with at most two effects, otherwise `"laplace"` |

With `nAGQ = 1` the quadrature is the Laplace approximation. The estimates
equal those of `lme4::glmer()` (Poisson) and `glmmTMB` (Poisson, NB1 and
NB2) with the same approximation.

## 12. Related models

* `countreg_rp()` fits random parameters at one level, with free means and
  non-normal distributions (lognormal, triangular, gamma, ...) and
  heterogeneity in their means and variances, by simulation.
* `renb()`, `repois()` and `poislind_re()` fit random effects with
  conjugate distributions in closed form.
* `countreg_fe()` fits fixed-effects models, which make no assumption about
  how the group effects relate to the covariates.

## 13. Not yet available

Non-normal random effects at more than one level (nested simulation),
smooth terms in the distribution-parameter formulas, and `te()` and `ti()`
smooths (use `t2()`) are not yet available in `countreg_hier()`.
